overview: Tula in central Mexico was a major city of craftspeople, traders and monumental builders. Its political reach remains debated: connections through objects and stories do not by themselves establish the borders of a Toltec empire.

periods.title: Building the Tollan city
periods.summary: Tula Grande developed as the principal monumental centre. Excavation links urban growth with substantial building activity and expanding pottery production.

periods.title: The later Tollan phase
periods.summary: Changing pottery assemblages distinguish the later phase. The revised chronology places the end of the Tollan city around 1150, rather than fixing a universally accepted fall date.

periods.title: People return to the ruins
periods.summary: The succeeding Fuego phase includes visits and deposits at an already ruined monumental centre. Such activity does not establish uninterrupted occupation of the former city.

items.text: An excavated obsidian workshop combined residential compounds, refuse dumps and probable outdoor working spaces. Microscopic fragments in soil helped identify places where stone was worked. Production took place within a lived environment, not only inside monumental buildings.

The workshop received large, roughly prepared obsidian cores from more than one source. Craftspeople reduced them into cores for narrow blades, blades themselves and further blade products. The discarded pieces preserve stages of this skilled manufacturing sequence.

Tohil plumbate vessels at Tula connect the city with pottery production in Chiapas and Guatemala. Tracing where ceramics were made reveals routes of exchange; finding a foreign vessel does not show that its makers were governed from Tula.

Potters used multiple brushes together to paint repeated lines, and moulds helped produce vessels efficiently. Excavated moulds turn a proposed manufacturing technique into a directly documented practice.

At rural Tepetitlán, hearths and cooking vessels identify areas where meals were prepared and eaten. A patio also contained an altar and other activity remains, suggesting that ordinary work and shared ritual occupied connected domestic spaces.

Tepetitlán yielded many cooking pots but few fragments of the usual griddle type. The researcher offered alternative explanations, including use of other vessels. Archaeology cannot turn this small sample into certainty that residents did, or did not, make tortillas.

Carbonised maize stems and roots at Tepetitlán provide evidence for cultivation and burning harvested fields. Other remains include amaranth and wild plants such as prickly pear and mesquite. Their survival helps reconstruct resources without supplying a complete household diet.

The plant study also identified materials used as fuel, including thorny shrubs, yucca and prickly pear. Keeping a hearth burning required knowledge of the surrounding dry landscape, alongside the work of raising crops.

Human-shaped columns on Pyramid B once supported a temple roof. Carved equipment includes spearthrowers and butterfly-shaped breastplates, while surviving pigment shows that the figures were coloured. Structure and representation worked together.

A clay warrior wearing a jaguar helmet was fired and inlaid with mother-of-pearl. Pohl connects its shell material with the Gulf of California. The object combines modelling, firing and inlay with access to distant materials.

Reclining sculptures known as chacmools turn their heads sideways and support a receptacle on the abdomen. Tula’s architectural friezes also feature jaguars, coyotes, eagles and feathered serpents, placing powerful imagery within public ceremonial settings.

Housing varied in scale, construction and location. The museum describes groups of rooms arranged around shared patios, where domestic and ritual activities could take place. The city’s inhabitants did not all live in one standard kind of house.

ending.text: The Tollan city was abandoned and monumental buildings burned, but these were not necessarily one event. The 2021 study leaves the destroyers unidentified. Later visitors and settlers reused the ruins, so political collapse did not erase the place or its significance.

sources.title: Dan M. Healan, Robert H. Cobean and Robert T. Bowsher, Revised Chronology and Settlement History of Tula and the Tula Region (2021)
sources.note: Pages 176 to 181: pottery manufacture, revised Tollan phases, abandonment and later visits. Dates remain archaeological estimates.

sources.title: John Pohl, FAMSI: Tula
sources.note: Compound layout, imports and painted sculpture. Later legends and imported objects do not establish imperial borders.

sources.note: Abstract and excavation report: residential workshop, soil analysis and imported cores; conclusions concern the excavated complex.

sources.title: Robert H. Cobean and Alba Guadalupe Mastache, editors, Tepetitlán: A Rural Household in the Toltec Heartland (1999)
sources.note: Moncayo Ochoa, ceramic analysis; González Quintero, plant remains. Excavated household evidence, not a universal menu or exact recipe.
